SOURCE: "HyperAgents", Jenny Zhang, Bingchen Zhao, Wannan Yang, Jakob Foerster, Jeff Clune, Minqi Jiang, Sam Devlin, Tatiana Shavrina (UBC, Vector, Edinburgh, NYU, FAIR/Meta). arXiv:2603.19461v1, preprint, 19 Mar 2026 (PDF dated 23 Mar 2026). Code: github.com/facebookresearch/Hyperagents.

COVERAGE: 214,473 chars extracted (the first call reported 212,492). I read the main text (abstract through limitations, about chars 0-62,300), appendix A (initial agent, parent selection, pseudocode), B (baseline pseudocode, table 1; the rest was skimmed), C.2/C.4 splits, D (all), E.2, E.3 (headings plus E.3.2, E.3.3, E.3.7 in full), E.4, E.5 and F. I skipped these:
- the long E.1 code dumps of best-found agents (lines ~2047-2885);
- the Polyglot and robotics prompt listings in C;
- the remaining E.3 snippets (E.3.1, E.3.4-E.3.6);
- the reference list, only skimmed.
The figures.py captions script returned nothing. The captions below come from the text extraction. Extraction was clean.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Metacognitive self-modification (the improvement procedure is itself editable) lets the system improve in non-coding domains where the original DGM stays at about zero.
  number: DGM test 0.0 on paper review and 0.0 on robotics; DGM-custom 0.590 and 0.348; DGM-H 0.710 and 0.372.
  setup: 5 runs, medians with 95% bootstrap CI, 100 iterations, held-out test tasks. Paper review is accept/reject on 100 test papers (ICLR 2024/25, NeurIPS 2023/24). Robotics test is a zero-shot reward for torso height; training is walking forward. The initial agent scores 0.0 and 0.060. The DGM-H beats the DGM at p<0.05.
  quote: "On test tasks, DGM-H improves paper review performance from 0.0 (the initial agent) to 0.710 (CI: 0.590 – 0.750)"; "On robotics reward design, DGM-H improves performance from 0.060 (the initial agent) to 0.372 (CI: 0.355 – 0.436)"; "the original DGM achieves test-set performance of 0.0 (CI: 0.0 – 0.510) on paper review and 0.0 (CI: 0.0 – 0.090) on robotics reward design"; "DGM-custom achieves substantially stronger results: 0.590 (CI: 0.570 – 0.650) on paper review and 0.348 (CI: 0.305 – 0.385)"
  where: Sec 5.1, about chars 33-37k, pp. 8-9
- claim: The DGM-H beats the handcrafted DGM-custom only on median; the difference is not significant.
  number: p>0.05
  quote: "The DGM-H achieves higher median performance than DGM-custom on the test tasks in both domains, although the difference is not statistically significant (p > 0.05)"
  where: Sec 5.1, p. 9
- claim: Both ablations stall. Removing self-improvement (the ADAS-like fixed meta agent) or removing the archive kills progress.
  number: w/o self-improve 0.0 and 0.213; w/o open-ended 0.0 and 0.116
  setup: as above, 100 iterations. DGM-H is significantly better than both (p<0.05). The w/o-open-ended paper review CI is 0.0-0.560, so it is wide.
  quote: "DGM-H w/o self-improve (Hu et al., 2025) shows little to no improvement, achieving test-set performance of 0.0 (CI: 0.0 – 0.130) on paper review and 0.213 (CI: 0.180 – 0.348) on robotics reward design."; "test-set performance remaining at 0.0 (CI: 0.0 – 0.560) on paper review and 0.116 (CI: 0.0 – 0.348) on robotics reward design"
  where: Sec 5.1, p. 9
- claim: Meta-level skill transfers across domains. A hyperagent evolved on paper review and robotics generates improved math-grading agents; DGM-custom transfer agents and the initial meta agent do not.
  number: imp@50 = 0.630 (CI 0.540-0.630) for DGM-H transfer versus 0.0 for the initial agent (DGM: 0.0, DGM-H: 0.0, CI 0.0-0.130) and 0.0 (CI 0.0-0.010) for DGM-custom transfer
  setup: IMO-GradingBench subset, 100 test tasks, 50 iterations, meta agent held fixed (w/o self-improve), 5 runs. Transfer agents are picked by a lineage-discounted growth score. o4-mini is the task model; Claude 4.5 Sonnet does the self-modification. p<0.05 versus the initial agent.
  quote: "After 50 iterations of DGM-H w/o self-improve starting from the transfer hyperagents, the best generated agents (selected based on validation score) achieve a test-set score of 0.630 (CI: 0.540 – 0.630). This corresponds to a imp@50 of 0.630 (CI: 0.540 – 0.630)"
  where: Sec 5.2, p. 10-11
- claim: Compounding across runs is only suggestive. Starting from transfer agents gives a higher median than starting fresh, but the difference is not significant.
  number: 0.640 (CI 0.550-0.720) versus 0.610 (CI 0.510-0.680), p>0.05
  setup: 200 iterations on math grading, best agent by validation, 5 runs
  quote: "achieve a test-set score of 0.640 (CI: 0.550 – 0.720). Under the same experimental setup, DGM-H starting from the initial agent achieves a best test-set score of 0.610 (CI: 0.510 – 0.680). Although the difference ... is not statistically significant (p > 0.05)"
  where: Sec 5.3, p. 12
- claim: Starting from the static ProofAutoGrader plus a transfer meta agent, the DGM-H yields a modestly better grader.
  number: test 0.700 vs 0.670; full IMO-GradingBench accuracy 0.561 to 0.601; MAE 0.178 to 0.175
  setup: 200 iterations. The 0.700 versus 0.670 figure is on the 100-task test split. The full-benchmark numbers come from E.4; the paper reports no CI or significance for them.
  quote: "On the full IMO-GradingBench, the DGM-H improves ProofAutoGrader's accuracy from 0.561 to 0.601, and lowers the mean absolute error from 0.178 to 0.175"
  where: Sec 5.3, p. 13
- claim: Coding parity with the original DGM, without a coding-specific design.
  number: Polyglot training subset 0.140 to 0.340; full benchmark 0.084 to 0.267. The DGM had 0.140 to 0.380 and 0.142 to 0.307.
  setup: 80 iterations, same FMs as the DGM (Claude 3.5 Sonnet new for self-modification, o3-mini for evaluation), 5 runs. Note the different full-benchmark starting points (0.084 versus 0.142).
  quote: "the DGM-H improves its training performance on the 50-task Polyglot subset from 0.140 (the initial agent) to 0.340 (CI: 0.300 – 0.380). ... performance increases from 0.084 (the initial agent) to 0.267 (CI: 0.231 – 0.280)"
  where: Sec 5.1, p. 7
- claim: Without being told to, the hyperagent built its own meta-tooling: performance tracking, persistent memory, bias detection, compute-aware planning (changing strategy by iterations remaining).
  number: in one observed case a 99% accept rate gave 49% accuracy, which became 63% after bias correction
  setup: qualitative, from single runs, with no ablation of each mechanism
  quote: "paper review predictions exhibited a 99% acceptance rate, yielding near-random accuracy of 49%. After bias detection and correction, the predictions became more balanced and accuracy improved to 63%."
  where: App E.3.3, p. 52
- claim: The task-level gains were structural rather than attitudinal. A "rigorous reviewer" persona was unreliable. Gen 54's insight was "use structured processes, not attitude instructions", leading to a two-stage checklist-then-decision pipeline. For robotics, the gain came from environment documentation (gen 8) that removed hallucinated attributes. For math grading, rubrics and a decision tree appeared at gen 168.
  number: none
  quote: "for LLMs, use structured processes, not attitude instructions"
  where: App E.2, p. 48
- claim: Letting the DGM-H modify parent selection beats random selection but not the handcrafted rule. It reinvents UCB, softmax and stagnation detection.
  number: random 0.428 (CI 0.407-0.432); modifiable 0.491 (CI 0.387-0.512); handcrafted score-child-prop 0.532 (CI 0.384-0.586); p>0.05
  setup: paper review plus robotics, test average, 5 runs, initial agent 0.030
  quote: "Allowing the DGM-H to modify the parent selection mechanism further improves performance to 0.491 (CI: 0.387 – 0.512). The handcrafted score-child-prop parent selection achieves the highest performance, improving from 0.030 to 0.532 (CI: 0.384–0.586)."
  where: App E.5, p. 57
- claim: Cost. A 100-iteration run costs about 88.6M tokens, of which 33M are self-modification.
  quote: "the estimated total cost is 33M tokens for self-modification plus 0.506M×100 for evaluation, yielding a total of approximately 88.6M tokens"
  where: App D.2, p. 35
- claim: BetterGrader's gain comes from fewer extreme-label collapses. Accuracy is +4.06%, Almost recall +18.52%, Correct recall -6.00%.
  quote: "the net effect is higher overall accuracy (+4.06%)"
  where: App E.4, p. 56

MECHANISM (for the note)
- A hyperagent is one editable program holding a task agent and a meta agent. The initial meta agent's prompt is just "Modify any part of the codebase at `{repo_path}`." It gets bash plus a file-edit tool, the path to previous evaluations, and the number of iterations remaining.
- The loop: select parents, self-modify, evaluate, add to the archive if it compiles (Algorithm 1).
- Parent selection: sigmoid(λ=10) of score around the mean of the top-3 scores, times 1/(1+compiled children), sampled with replacement (A.2). This selector is held fixed in the main experiments.
- Staged evaluation to save cost: 10 tasks first, then the full set only if at least one succeeds; failures score zero. For multi-domain runs, failing either domain skips the full training set for both.
- imp@k = max test score among up to k generated agents (chosen by validation score), minus the starting agent's score, with the meta agent held fixed.
- Transfer-agent selection: discounted descendant growth G_γ(i) = mean over descendants of (α_j − α_i)·γ^dist, with γ=0.6 and at least 3 descendants.

LIMITS
- The authors concede: the task distribution is fixed. Parent selection and evaluation protocols are outside the editable program, so it is not fully self-referential. The "unbounded" talk is aspirational.
- Safety (Sec 6, App F): sandboxing with resource limits and human oversight were used throughout. They name evaluation gaming (Goodhart) and amplified human bias, and say that safeguards "may become increasingly strained".
- Weak statistics: 5 runs per method. Several headline comparisons are not significant (DGM-H vs DGM-custom; the transfer-compounding result; the parent-selection result). The CIs for some baselines are very wide.
- Compounding evidence is thin: one source domain pair, one target domain, a 0.03 median gain.
- The paper-review "ground truth" is noisy human decisions. The 0.710 beats an AI-Scientist-v2 reviewer baseline of 0.630 (Sec 5.1 says "several top-performing agents outperform" it, so not all of them do).
- The initial agents score 0.0 partly because of output-format parsing failures, which inflates the gains from the first fixes (stated by the authors).
- Test splits are 100 tasks each, so scores are coarse.
- imp@k is linear and ignores saturation (D.3).
- The qualitative meta-improvements are single-run anecdotes. There is no ablation showing that memory or tracking causes the transfer.
- Dated: models are Claude 4.5 Sonnet, o4-mini, GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Everything is a preprint with no peer review noted.

BUILDS ON: Darwin Gödel Machine (Zhang et al., 2025b), the archive and stepping stones; ADAS (Hu, Lu, Clune, 2025), the fixed-meta-agent baseline; Gödel Machine (Schmidhuber, 2003); Kirsch and Schmidhuber (2022), self-referential meta-learning; Go-Explore (Ecoffet et al., 2019), parent selection; Eureka (Ma et al., 2024), robotics reward design; AI-Scientist-v2 (Yamada et al., 2025), reviewer baseline; IMO-GradingBench / ProofAutoGrader (Luong et al., 2025); Polyglot (Gauthier, 2024); Zhao et al. (2026), paper-review dataset; Genesis (2024) simulator; UCB (Auer et al., 2002), rediscovered by the agent; Huxley-Gödel Machine (Wang et al., 2025b), related work.

CODE (verbatim, from the text)
- Initial meta agent prompt (App A.1): instruction = f"Modify any part of the codebase at ‘{repo_path}‘."
- Initial task agent prompt (App A.1): "You are an agent. Task input: ... Respond in JSON format with the following schema: <json>{{"response": ...}}</json>"
- Algorithm 1 core (App A.3): a′←a.Modify(a,A) // Metacognitive self-modification; s′←Evaluate(a′,T); if IsValid(a′) then A←A∪{(a′,s′)}
- Emergent bias detector (App E.3.3): if ratio > 0.8: # Threshold for bias detection ... bias_info += f"\n\n### BIAS DETECTED in {gen}/{domain}:"
- Emergent compute-aware guidance (E.3.2): if iterations_left > 5: "You have many iterations remaining. Consider making fundamental improvements ..."; elif iterations_left > 2: "... Refining existing mechanisms"; else: "... Conservative, high-confidence improvements"
- PerformanceTracker class (Sec 5.2, p. 11-12): record_generation(generation_id, domain, score, metadata) and get_improvement_trend(domain, window=5), which returns recent_avg - older_avg. It is in the text and too long to copy here.
- MemoryTool with store/retrieve/list_keys writing a timestamped memory.json (E.3.7).
- Evolved UCB (E.5): exploration_bonus = exploration_weight * math.sqrt(math.log(total_children + 1) / (children + 1)); ucb_score = normalized_score + exploration_bonus

FIGURES (captions per text extraction; page numbers from the footer)
- Fig 1 (p. 4): DGM versus DGM-H architecture. The DGM has a fixed, handcrafted instruction generator and aligned eval and self-modification tasks; in the DGM-H the task and meta agent form one editable program. This is the best single diagram for the note.
- Fig 2 (p. 8): training and test curves for paper review and robotics, DGM-H versus DGM, DGM-custom, w/o self-improve, w/o open-ended. It shows that every component is needed.
- Fig 3 (p. 10): imp@50 bars, 0.0 for the baselines versus 0.630 for the transfer hyperagent. This is the clearest evidence of learned meta skill.
- Fig 4 (p. 13): math grading with and without transfer, plus ProofAutoGrader initialisation.
- Fig 7-9 (pp. 49-50): archive trees annotated with the code change per key node (persona, then two-stage; env docs; rubric and decision tree). They show non-monotone lineages through weaker stepping stones.
- Fig 10 (p. 56): confusion matrices for ProofAutoGrader versus BetterGrader.
- Fig 11-12 (pp. 57, 59): modifiable parent selection.
- Table 1 (B): method versus feature matrix (self-improving meta, open-ended archive, metacognitive).

PROBLEMS: Extraction is clean apart from minor spacing in code and equations. No embedded instructions found. The figures captions script produced no output. I did not read the E.1 agent code dumps, so I make no claims about their contents. The numbers for the full-benchmark gains (0.561 to 0.601) are quoted from Sec 5.3 only.
